description: The grammar points that most often trip up non-native professionals: tenses (present perfect, continuous, future forms), articles, uncountable nouns, gerunds vs infinitives, question word order, conditionals, polite modals, prepositions, and common mistakes, with workplace examples.

cards.front: Correct this: 'I have did the code review yesterday.'
cards.back: I did the code review yesterday.
cards.explanation: Yesterday = simple past (did). Present perfect (have done) doesn't take a finished time like yesterday.
cards.example: I reviewed it yesterday. I've already left a comment.

cards.front: Correct this: 'He don't has access to production.'
cards.back: He doesn't have access to production.
cards.explanation: Third person: doesn't + base verb. Have, not has, after doesn't.
cards.example: She doesn't have permission to merge to main.

cards.front: Correct this: 'We was blocked by the API change.'
cards.back: We were blocked by the API change.
cards.explanation: We/you/they + were. I/he/she/it + was.
cards.example: They were blocked until the contract tests passed.

cards.front: Correct this: 'Please explain me the stack trace.'
cards.back: Please explain the stack trace to me.
cards.explanation: Explain doesn't take a person as a direct object.
cards.example: Can you explain the stack trace to me?

cards.front: Present perfect vs past simple: when do you use each?
cards.back: Past simple for a finished time (yesterday, last week, in 2023, at 3 pm). Present perfect for past actions connected to now, with no finished time: experience, results, or 'up to now' (already, yet, ever, just, so far, this week).
cards.explanation: If you can say when, use past simple. 'I have finished it yesterday' is wrong. Present perfect focuses on the present result: 'I've fixed the bug' (it's fixed now).
cards.example: I've deployed the fix. (result now) / I deployed it at 10 a.m. (finished time) / Have you ever used Kotlin?

cards.front: Where do 'already' and 'yet' go, and which tense do they usually take?
cards.back: Usually the present perfect. 'Yet' goes at the end of questions and negatives; 'already' goes in positive sentences, usually before the main verb. (American English also accepts past simple: 'Did you finish yet?')
cards.explanation: I've already merged it. / I haven't merged it yet. / Have you merged it yet? 'Already' in a question shows surprise: 'Have you already finished?!'
cards.example: The PR isn't approved yet, but I've already fixed the comments.

cards.front: When do you use the present perfect continuous (have been doing)?
cards.back: For an activity that started in the past and is still going on or just stopped, emphasizing duration: 'I've been working on this bug for two days.'
cards.explanation: Compare: 'I've been fixing tests all morning' (activity, maybe not done) vs 'I've fixed five tests' (completed results, a number). Stative verbs (know, like, own) don't use the continuous: 'I've known him for years'.
cards.example: We've been waiting for the security review since Monday.

cards.front: How do you talk about future plans: 'will', 'going to', or present continuous?
cards.back: Present continuous for fixed arrangements (I'm meeting the client on Friday). 'Going to' for plans already decided and predictions from evidence (I'm going to refactor this; the build is going to fail). 'Will' for decisions made now, offers, and promises (I'll check it).
cards.explanation: In meetings, 'I'll take that' (deciding now) sounds natural. 'I will take that' with full 'will' sounds formal or insistent.
cards.example: A: Who can update the docs? B: I'll do it. (decision now) / I'm going to update the docs tomorrow. (already planned)

cards.front: Past continuous vs past simple in a story?
cards.back: Past continuous (was/were doing) sets the background action in progress; past simple is the shorter event that happened during it.
cards.explanation: This is the most natural way to describe incidents. Use 'when' before the past simple event and 'while' before the continuous background.
cards.example: I was deploying the release when the database went down. / While we were testing, the server restarted.

cards.front: 'A' or 'an' before abbreviations like API, SQL, URL, HTTP?
cards.back: Choose by the first sound, not the letter: an API (ay), an HTTP request (aitch), an SQL query if you say 'ess-cue-el' but a SQL query if you say 'sequel', a URL (you), a user (you), an hour (silent h), a one-time token (wun).
cards.explanation: 'An' goes before a vowel sound, 'a' before a consonant sound. Both 'a SQL' and 'an SQL' appear in writing because people pronounce it differently.
cards.example: We need an API key and a URL for the webhook. It takes an hour.

cards.front: When do you use 'the', and when no article at all?
cards.back: 'The' for something specific that both speakers know (the build, the bug I mentioned, the main branch). No article for plural or uncountable nouns used in general (Developers love coffee. Security matters.).
cards.explanation: Common mistake from many languages: 'The developers love coffee' when you mean developers in general. Use 'a/an' to introduce a singular countable thing for the first time, then 'the' after.
cards.example: I found a bug in the login flow. The bug only happens on Safari. Bugs like this are hard to reproduce.

cards.front: Correct this: 'Can you give me some informations and advices about the softwares?'
cards.back: 'Can you give me some information and advice about the software?'
cards.explanation: Information, advice, feedback, software, hardware, equipment, research, knowledge, furniture, and homework are uncountable: no plural -s and no 'a'. To count them, use 'a piece of advice', 'a bit of feedback', 'two pieces of software', 'a tool'.
cards.example: Thanks for the feedback! One more piece of advice: add tests.

cards.front: Is it 'codes' or 'code'?
cards.back: 'Code' as programming source is uncountable: 'I wrote some code', 'a lot of code', 'a piece of code / a snippet'. 'Codes' is only for separate identifiers: error codes, status codes, promo codes.
cards.explanation: 'Please review my codes' is a very common non-native mistake. Say 'my code', 'my changes', or 'my PR'.
cards.example: This code returns three different error codes.

cards.front: Much or many? Fewer or less? Few or little?
cards.back: Countable nouns: many, few, fewer (many bugs, fewer meetings). Uncountable nouns: much, little, less (much time, less traffic).
cards.explanation: 'Less meetings' is very common in speech, but 'fewer meetings' is correct in careful writing. In positive sentences 'a lot of' sounds more natural than 'much': 'We have a lot of work' not 'We have much work'.
cards.example: We have fewer incidents and less downtime this quarter. How many tickets are left? How much time do we have?

cards.front: Which common verbs take -ing after them?
cards.back: enjoy, avoid, suggest, recommend, consider, mind, finish, keep, practice, risk, deny, can't help, look forward to.
cards.explanation: 'I suggest to use a map' is wrong: 'I suggest using a map' or 'I suggest that we use a map'. 'Look forward to' ends with the preposition 'to', so it takes -ing: 'I look forward to hearing from you'.
cards.example: Would you mind sharing your screen? I recommend adding a retry. I look forward to working with you.

cards.front: Which common verbs take 'to + verb' after them?
cards.back: want, need, decide, plan, agree, hope, expect, promise, refuse, manage, offer, seem, tend, would like.
cards.explanation: 'I want that you review it' is wrong: 'I want you to review it'. Same pattern: need/expect/ask someone to do something.
cards.example: We decided to postpone the release. I'd like you to take a look. She managed to fix it before the demo.

cards.front: What's the difference: 'stop doing' vs 'stop to do', 'remember doing' vs 'remember to do'?
cards.back: 'Stop doing' = quit the activity; 'stop to do' = pause in order to do something else. 'Remember doing' = have a memory of it; 'remember to do' = not forget a future task. 'Forget' and 'try' change meaning the same way.
cards.explanation: 'Try restarting it' = experiment with this solution. 'Try to restart it' = make an effort (it might be hard).
cards.example: We stopped using Jenkins. / He stopped to answer a call. / Remember to rotate the keys. / I remember fixing this before.

cards.front: Make or do?
cards.back: 'Do' for tasks, work, and activities in general: do a review, do the dishes, do research, do your best, do a favor. 'Make' for creating or producing something, and decisions: make a decision, make a mistake, make a change, make progress, make a call, make sure.
cards.explanation: These are fixed collocations; learn them as chunks. 'Do a mistake' and 'make a research' are common errors.
cards.example: We made good progress, but we need to make a decision before we do the migration.

cards.front: Say or tell?
cards.back: 'Tell' needs a person: tell someone something. 'Say' doesn't take a person directly: say something (to someone).
cards.explanation: 'He said me that...' is wrong: 'He told me that...' or 'He said that...'. Fixed: tell the truth, tell a story, tell the difference; say hello, say sorry.
cards.example: She told me the build was broken. She said it was broken. Can you tell the difference?

cards.front: Correct this: 'Can you tell me where is the config file?'
cards.back: 'Can you tell me where the config file is?'
cards.explanation: Indirect (embedded) questions use statement word order: no inversion and no do/does/did. 'Do you know what time it starts?' not 'what time does it start?'. Use 'if' or 'whether' for yes/no: 'Do you know if the API is down?'
cards.example: Could you explain why the test fails? Do you know whether we support Java 21?

cards.front: Correct this: 'What this method does?' and 'Why you didn't push?'
cards.back: 'What does this method do?' and 'Why didn't you push?'
cards.explanation: Direct questions need an auxiliary (do/does/did, is, have, can) before the subject. Exception: when the question word is the subject itself: 'Who broke the build?' (no 'did').
cards.example: Where do you store the secrets? What happened? Who approved this PR?

cards.front: Correct this: 'I'm working here since 2022.'
cards.back: 'I've been working here since 2022.' (or 'I've worked here since 2022.')
cards.explanation: For a situation that started in the past and continues now, English uses present perfect, not present simple or continuous. 'Since' + starting point; 'for' + length of time.
cards.example: I've known her for five years. We've used Kafka since last spring.

cards.front: Correct this: 'If I would have known, I would have told you.'
cards.back: 'If I had known, I would have told you.'
cards.explanation: Third conditional (imaginary past): If + past perfect, would have + past participle. Never 'would' in the if-clause. In speech: 'If I'd known, I'd have told you.'
cards.example: If we had added an alert, we would have caught it earlier.

cards.front: Zero, first, and second conditionals: what's the difference?
cards.back: Zero (always true): If + present, present — If the cache is cold, requests are slow. First (real future): If + present, will — If the tests pass, I'll merge. Second (imaginary or unlikely now): If + past, would — If we had more time, we would rewrite it.
cards.explanation: Don't use 'will' in the if-clause: 'If it will rain' is wrong. 'Unless' = if not: 'Don't merge unless the build is green.'
cards.example: If I were the tech lead, I'd split this service. (second, imaginary)

cards.front: How do modal verbs make requests more polite?
cards.back: From direct to polite: 'Can you...?' → 'Could you...?' → 'Would you mind ...ing?' → 'I was wondering if you could...'
cards.explanation: Past forms (could, would, was wondering) add distance, which sounds softer in English. 'Would you mind' expects -ing, and you answer 'No, not at all' to say yes.
cards.example: I was wondering if you could take a look at my PR when you have a moment.

cards.front: When should you use the passive voice at work?
cards.back: When the action matters more than who did it, the actor is unknown, or naming a person would sound like blame: 'The bug was introduced in version 2.3.'
cards.explanation: In postmortems, passive and system-focused language keeps things blameless. Elsewhere, prefer active voice; it's clearer and shorter: 'We fixed the bug' rather than 'The bug was fixed by us'.
cards.example: The config was changed at 14:02, and the service was restarted automatically.

cards.front: How does reported speech work?
cards.back: Usually shift the tense back one step after a past reporting verb: 'The build is failing' → She said (that) the build was failing. 'We will deploy' → He said they would deploy.
cards.explanation: If the fact is still true now, you can keep the present: 'She said the service is down' (it's still down). Questions become statements: 'He asked if I had pushed'.
cards.example: The PM said they needed it by Friday. He asked when we could release.

cards.front: Who, which, or that, and when do you need commas?
cards.back: Who for people, which for things, that for both in defining clauses. Non-defining clauses (extra information, with commas) use who or which, never that.
cards.explanation: Defining: 'The service that handles payments is down' (which service? this one). Non-defining: 'The payment service, which we migrated last year, is down' (extra detail).
cards.example: The engineer who wrote this has left. Our API, which is public, needs versioning.

cards.front: It's vs its, there / their / they're, your / you're, then / than?
cards.back: it's = it is; its = belonging to it. there = place; their = belonging to them; they're = they are. you're = you are; your = belonging to you. then = time/next; than = comparison.
cards.explanation: Native speakers also mix these up in writing, but in documentation and emails they look careless. Read your message once before sending.
cards.example: It's faster than the old version; its memory use is lower too. They're moving their service over there.

cards.front: Affect vs effect, lose vs loose?
cards.back: 'Affect' is usually a verb (to influence); 'effect' is usually a noun (the result). 'Lose' = not have anymore; 'loose' = not tight.
cards.explanation: Memory trick: Affect = Action (verb), Effect = End result (noun). 'Loose coupling' (correct) vs 'we might lose data' (correct).
cards.example: The outage affected 5% of users. The effect on revenue was small. We don't want to lose any messages.

cards.front: Prepositions of time: in, on, or at?
cards.back: at + clock times and specific points (at 3 pm, at noon, at the end of the sprint). on + days and dates (on Monday, on May 5). in + months, years, seasons, parts of the day, and 'after a period' (in March, in 2026, in the morning, in two days).
cards.explanation: 'In two days' = two days from now. 'Within two days' = any time before two days have passed. No preposition before next, last, this, every: 'next Monday', not 'on next Monday'.
cards.example: The release is on Friday at 10. I'll reply in an hour. We deploy every Tuesday.

cards.front: Correct this: 'I am agree with you' and 'It is depend on the load.'
cards.back: 'I agree with you.' and 'It depends on the load.'
cards.explanation: Agree and depend are normal verbs, not adjectives, so no 'am/is' before them. Negative: 'I don't agree' or 'I disagree'.
cards.example: I agree that we need a cache, but the size depends on the traffic.

cards.front: Correct this: 'This approach is more better and more faster.'
cards.back: 'This approach is better and faster.'
cards.explanation: Short adjectives take -er (faster, cheaper) and long ones take 'more' (more reliable), never both. Irregular: good → better → best, bad → worse → worst. Comparisons use 'than': 'faster than before'.
cards.example: Redis is faster than the database, but the database is more reliable for this data.

cards.front: Where do frequency adverbs (always, usually, often, never) go?
cards.back: Before the main verb, but after 'be' and after the first auxiliary: 'I always check the logs.' / 'The build is usually green.' / 'I have never seen this error.'
cards.explanation: 'I check always the logs' is a common word-order error. 'Sometimes' can also go at the start: 'Sometimes the test fails.'
cards.example: We usually deploy on Tuesdays, but we never deploy on Fridays.

cards.front: 'Used to do' vs 'be used to doing'?
cards.back: 'Used to + verb' = a past habit that's no longer true. 'Be / get used to + -ing' = be / become familiar with something.
cards.explanation: 'I'm used to work late' is wrong: 'I'm used to working late'. Negative past habit: 'We didn't use to have code reviews' (no -d after didn't).
cards.example: We used to deploy manually. I'm still getting used to working with Kotlin.

cards.front: Subject-verb agreement traps: 'The list of users is/are', 'Everyone has/have', 'The team is/are'?
cards.back: 'The list of users is' (the subject is 'list'). 'Everyone has' (everyone, someone, nobody, each take singular verbs). 'The team is' in American English; British English also allows 'the team are'.
cards.explanation: Find the real subject, skipping the 'of ...' phrase. 'Data is' and 'data are' are both accepted; 'data is' is more common in tech.
cards.example: Each of the services has its own database. The number of errors is rising.

cards.front: What is a comma splice, and how do you fix it in writing?
cards.back: Joining two complete sentences with only a comma: 'The build failed, I fixed it.' Fix with a period, a semicolon, or a conjunction: 'The build failed, so I fixed it.'
cards.explanation: Very common in chat, but in docs, tickets, and emails it reads as sloppy. Short sentences are usually clearer anyway.
cards.example: The deploy is done. Monitoring looks normal, but I'll keep an eye on error rates.

cards.text: Let's discuss {{c1::the}} rollout plan.
cards.extra: Discuss + object. Don't say 'discuss about'.

cards.text: This change depends {{c1::on}} the auth service.
cards.extra: Depend on + noun. Not 'depend of' or 'depend from'.

cards.text: I'm responsible {{c1::for}} the payment module.
cards.extra: Responsible for + noun or -ing. Not 'responsible of'.

cards.text: We're waiting {{c1::for}} the pipeline to finish.
cards.extra: Wait for someone/something. 'Wait on' is possible but less common here.

cards.text: Could you explain this {{c1::to}} me?
cards.extra: Explain something to someone. Not 'explain me this'.

cards.text: I suggest {{c1::adding}} a null check.
cards.extra: Suggest + -ing, or suggest that we add. Not 'suggest to add'.

cards.text: We need to avoid {{c1::shipping}} this without a test.
cards.extra: Avoid + -ing. Not 'avoid to ship'.

cards.text: I'm interested {{c1::in}} pairing on this.
cards.extra: Interested in + noun or -ing. Not 'interested on'.

cards.text: The bug has been open {{c1::for}} three days.
cards.extra: For + a duration. Since + a starting point (since Monday).

cards.text: I've been working on this {{c1::since}} Monday.
cards.extra: Since + a point in time. Use present perfect for something that started then and continues.

cards.text: If the build {{c1::fails}}, I'll fix it before standup.
cards.extra: First conditional for a real future: if + present, will + verb. Not 'if it will fail'.

cards.text: If I {{c1::were}} you, I'd split this class.
cards.extra: Second conditional for advice: if I were you, I'd... 'Were' is standard here, not 'was'.

cards.text: The tests passed, {{c1::so}} I merged the PR.
cards.extra: So + result. Because + reason. Don't use both: not 'because so'.

cards.text: I finished the fix, {{c1::but}} the integration test is still red.
cards.extra: But contrasts. And adds. So gives a result.

cards.text: I {{c1::have worked}} here for three years, and I {{c2::joined}} the platform team last year.
cards.extra: Present perfect for up-to-now duration; past simple for a finished time.

cards.text: Thanks for your {{c1::feedback}}; it was really useful.
cards.extra: Feedback is uncountable: no 'feedbacks', no 'a feedback'.

cards.text: I look forward to {{c1::hearing}} from you.
cards.extra: 'To' here is a preposition, so it takes -ing.

cards.text: Do you know where {{c1::the logs are}}?
cards.extra: Indirect questions use statement word order.

cards.text: We need to {{c1::make}} a decision before we {{c2::do}} the migration.
cards.extra: Make a decision / a mistake / progress; do a task / research / a review.

cards.text: The meeting is {{c1::on}} Monday {{c2::at}} 10 a.m.
cards.extra: On + days and dates; at + clock times; in + months and years.
